chapters.title: Chapter 2: The Bid-Ask Spread: What It Is Made Of

lessons.title: Decomposing the Spread: Order Processing, Inventory, and Adverse Selection Costs

body.text: The number quoted on screen as the bid-ask spread is not one cost. It is three completely different costs bundled into a single figure, and a market maker who cannot tell them apart cannot price any of them correctly.

children.text: Three Reasons a Market Maker Widens or Narrows a Quote

Market microstructure research, going back to classic studies of spreads on exchanges like the NYSE, converges on the same decomposition, and it applies just as well to a Nifty option quoted on NSE: the bid-ask spread compensates a market maker for three separate things at once. Order processing cost is the plain expense of running the operation. Inventory holding cost is the risk of being stuck with an unwanted position. Adverse selection cost is the risk of trading against someone who simply knows more than you do. Every quote a market maker posts is, whether it realises it explicitly or not, a single number trying to cover all three.

body.caption: The classic three-way decomposition of the bid-ask spread. Each term can move independently, and a market maker's quote is the sum of all three at any given instant.

children.text: Order Processing Cost: The Cost of Simply Running the Book

This is the least interesting of the three components and the most mechanical. It covers exchange transaction charges, clearing and settlement costs, technology and connectivity, compliance, and the ordinary overhead of operating a quoting business. It does not depend on which way the market is likely to move or on who is on the other side of the trade; it exists purely because running the business costs money, and that cost has to be recovered somewhere in the price charged for immediacy.

body.text: This is exactly the component that SEBI's Liquidity Enhancement Scheme, from the previous chapter, is designed to shrink. Waiving exchange transaction charges for an appointed market maker lowers its order processing cost directly, which is precisely why an LES-appointed market maker can afford to quote a tighter spread on an illiquid contract than the underlying economics would otherwise support.

children.text: Inventory Holding Cost: The Cost of Being Stuck With a Position

markDefs.definition: The risk a market maker bears from the moment its quote is hit until it can offload the resulting position, arising because the market can move against that position in the meantime. It is compensated for by widening the spread, and it grows with volatility and with how long the position is expected to be held.

children.text: Every time a market maker's bid or ask gets hit, it ends up holding a position it did not choose the timing of. Between that moment and whenever it manages to trade that position back off, the market can move against it. This is

, and unlike order processing cost, it is not fixed at all: it rises with the volatility of the instrument being quoted, and it rises the longer a position is expected to sit before it can be offloaded. A market maker quoting a Bank Nifty weekly option two hours before expiry, when gamma and realised volatility are both elevated, needs a wider spread to cover this risk than the same market maker quoting a far-dated, low-volatility contract.

body.label: Why Spreads Widen Into an Event
body.context: Ahead of a Union Budget, an RBI monetary policy announcement, or a large index constituent's results, expected volatility rises even before anything is announced. A market maker's inventory holding cost rises with it, which is why quoted spreads on Nifty and Bank Nifty options routinely widen in the hours before such events, independent of anything else changing.

children.text: Adverse Selection Cost: The Cost of Trading With Someone Who Knows More

A market maker cannot tell, in the instant an order hits its quote, whether the trader on the other side is an ordinary participant rebalancing a portfolio or someone trading on information the market maker does not yet have. Since it cannot tell the two apart, it has to price both possibilities into every quote it posts, which means charging everyone, informed and uninformed alike, a little more than order processing and inventory risk alone would justify. That extra charge is adverse selection cost, and it exists purely because information is unevenly distributed across market participants.

body.text: Of the three components, adverse selection is the one that can turn catastrophic rather than merely uncomfortable, because it does not average out the way ordinary trading risk does. A market maker facing a run of informed order flow loses systematically, on the same side, every time, until it either reprices or gets forced out. Chapter 4 is built entirely around detecting and pricing this risk properly.

body.text: These proportions are a stylised illustration of the general pattern classic microstructure research has found, not a measurement taken from NSE data. The actual split varies by instrument, by how informationally sensitive its underlying is, and by market conditions at the time; treat this chart as a way to remember that all three components exist and move independently, not as a number to rely on.

body.title: Widening the Quote Ahead of an RBI Policy Day
body.scenario: A market maker quoting Bank Nifty weekly options widens its spread noticeably in the two hours before an RBI monetary policy announcement, even though nothing has been announced yet and current realised volatility looks ordinary.
body.prompt: Using the three-way decomposition from this lesson, which components of the spread are most likely driving this widening, and why would order processing cost be the least likely explanation?
body.modelAnswer: Two components are doing almost all of the work here. Inventory holding cost rises because expected volatility around the announcement is higher than current realised volatility suggests, so any position taken on ahead of it carries more risk of an adverse move before it can be offloaded. Adverse selection cost also rises, since the probability that some incoming orders reflect information or positioning ahead of the policy outcome is higher than on an ordinary day, and the market maker cannot tell which specific orders those are. Order processing cost is the least likely explanation because it depends on exchange fees and operating costs, which do not change simply because a policy announcement is a few hours away.

body.title: Naming the Component
body.question: A market maker widens its spread specifically because it believes an unusually large share of the orders arriving right now come from traders who know something about an upcoming corporate announcement that it does not. Which component of the spread is this widening compensating for?
body.explanation: This is a direct description of adverse selection cost: the market maker cannot distinguish informed order flow from ordinary order flow, so it prices in the risk of trading against someone better informed by widening the spread for everyone. Inventory holding cost is about the risk of holding a resulting position through a volatile period, which is related but distinct from the information problem itself.

points: The bid-ask spread is the sum of three distinct costs: order processing, inventory holding, and adverse selection
Order processing cost is mechanical and largely fixed, covering exchange fees, technology, and compliance
Inventory holding cost rises with volatility and with how long a resulting position is expected to be held before it can be offloaded
Adverse selection cost exists because a market maker cannot tell informed order flow from uninformed order flow, so it prices in that uncertainty for everyone
SEBI's Liquidity Enhancement Scheme directly reduces order processing cost through fee waivers, which is one reason LES-appointed market makers can quote tighter
Spreads widening ahead of events like RBI policy announcements are typically driven by rising inventory and adverse selection cost, not by any change in order processing cost
